CHAPTER 4.2 · LEARNING AREA 4

CHAPTER 4.2 · LEARNING AREA 4 · APRIL · MAY

Cuboids

Shoebox, milk carton, brick, aquarium: cuboids are everywhere. You learn to draw a cuboid from the front, from above and from the side, as an oblique drawing and as a net. Then you calculate how much fits inside, the volume, and how much card you need for it, the surface area. Finally, in the project “Packaging”, you take a close look at real boxes.

14 LESSONS3 UNITS2 LABS
WHAT YOU WILL LEARN IN THIS CHAPTER
  • describe cuboids and cubes: vertices, edges, faces
  • show cuboids in views, as an oblique drawing and as a net, also solids made of several cuboids
  • calculate the volume of cuboids and convert units of volume and units of capacity
  • calculate the surface area and use it in the project “Packaging”

UNIT 14 LESSONS

1Drawing cuboids

Cut open, the box lies on the table as a connected figure made of six rectangles. A figure like this is called a net. Depending on which edges you cut open, you get different nets.

A cuboid has 8 vertices, 12 edges and 6 faces. All the faces are rectangles, and opposite faces are the same size. The edges are equal in length in groups of four. If all the edges are equal in length, the cuboid is a cube.

KEY POINT · WAYS OF DRAWING

Views: plan (from above), front view, side view. Every view is a rectangle.

Oblique drawing: The front face is drawn true to size. You draw the edges running towards the back at a slant of 45° and shortened. On squared paper you draw the diagonal of one square for 1 cm of depth. Hidden edges are dashed.

Net: all six faces connected in one plane, so that you can fold the cuboid from it.

Why shortened? What lies further back looks shorter to us. With the shortened edges the oblique drawing looks three-dimensional.

Eleven nets: A cube has exactly 11 different nets.

INTERACTIVE · OBLIQUE DRAWING AND NET
EXAMPLE 1 · VIEWS

A cuboid is 5 cm long, 3 cm wide and 2 cm high and lies flat on the table. Which rectangles do you see from above, from the front and from the right?

From above: 5 cm by 3 cm. From the front: 5 cm by 2 cm. From the right: 3 cm by 2 cm.

EXAMPLE 2 · SKELETON MODEL

A skeleton model of a cuboid with 6 cm, 4 cm and 3 cm is to be bent out of wire. How much wire do you need?

The edges are equal in length in groups of 4: $4 \cdot 6 + 4 \cdot 4 + 4 \cdot 3 = 4 \cdot 13 = 52$ cm.

52 cm

EXERCISES

Draw the oblique drawing of a cuboid with $a = 5$ cm, $b = 4$ cm and $c = 3$ cm on squared paper. Don’t forget the dashed lines!

Front face 5 cm by 3 cm, depth 4 cm as 4 diagonals of squares. Three edges at the bottom left at the back are hidden.

Draw two different nets of a cube with an edge length of 2 cm. Cut one out and fold it.

For example the cross (four squares in a row, one each above and below the second) and the staircase.

A cube has an edge length of 5 cm. How long are all the edges together? How many faces and edges meet at one vertex?

$12 \cdot 5 = 60$ cm. At every vertex 3 edges and 3 faces meet.

A solid is made of two cuboids: at the bottom 6 cm by 4 cm by 2 cm, and placed on top in the middle 2 cm by 2 cm by 3 cm. Draw the front view and the plan.

Front view: a rectangle 6 cm by 2 cm, with 2 cm by 3 cm on top in the middle (like an upside-down T). Plan: a rectangle 6 cm by 4 cm with a square 2 cm by 2 cm in the middle.

A cube is painted red on the outside and then cut into 27 equal small cubes. How many small cubes have 3, 2, 1 or 0 red faces?

3 red faces: 8 (vertices) · 2: 12 (middles of the edges) · 1: 6 (middles of the faces) · 0: 1 (right inside). Together 27.

TEST YOURSELF!

How many edges does a cuboid have?

4 of each length

Total edge length for 6 cm, 4 cm, 3 cm?

$4 \cdot (6 + 4 + 3)$

How do you draw the edges running towards the back in an oblique drawing?

slanting and shortened

UNIT 26 LESSONS

2Volume

The cuboid of interlocking cubes has 2 layers of $4 \cdot 3 = 12$ cubes each, so $2 \cdot 12 = 24$ cubes. You can calculate the volume of every cuboid like this.

The volume tells you how much space a solid takes up. You measure it with unit cubes: 1 cm³ is a cube with an edge length of 1 cm, about as big as a sugar cube.

KEY POINT · VOLUME OF A CUBOID

A cuboid with the edge lengths $a$, $b$ and $c$ has the volume $$V = a \cdot b \cdot c$$ A cube with the edge length $a$ has $V = a^3$.

Units of volume with the conversion factor 1000: 1 cm³ = 1000 mm³ · 1 dm³ = 1000 cm³ · 1 m³ = 1000 dm³

Units of capacity: 1 litre (l) = 1 dm³ · 1 millilitre (ml) = 1 cm³ · 1 hectolitre (hl) = 100 l

Why 1000? A cube with an edge length of 1 dm is 10 cm long, 10 cm wide and 10 cm high: $10 \cdot 10 \cdot 10 = 1000$ cm³.

One litre fits exactly into a cube with an edge length of 10 cm. So a one-litre milk carton has to hold at least 1,000 cm³.

INTERACTIVE · VOLUME FROM UNIT CUBES
INTERACTIVE · THE UNIT STAIRCASE FOR VOLUMES
EXAMPLE 3 · AQUARIUM

An aquarium is 60 cm long, 30 cm wide and 40 cm high. How many litres of water fit into it?

$V = 60 \cdot 30 \cdot 40 = 72{,}000$ cm³ $= 72$ dm³.

72 litres

EXAMPLE 4 · COMPOSITE

A stair landing consists of two cuboids: 3 m by 1 m by 0.2 m and 3 m by 0.5 m by 0.4 m. How much concrete do you need?

$3 \cdot 1 \cdot 0.2 = 0.6$ m³ and $3 \cdot 0.5 \cdot 0.4 = 0.6$ m³.

1.2 m³

EXERCISES

Calculate the volume: a) $a = 8$ cm, $b = 5$ cm, $c = 3$ cm   b) cube with $a = 6$ dm   c) $a = 2$ m, $b = 1.5$ m, $c = 1$ m

a) 120 cm³   b) 216 dm³   c) 3 m³

Convert: a) 4 dm³ into cm³   b) 2,500 cm³ into litres   c) 0.75 l into ml   d) 3 m³ into litres

a) 4,000 cm³   b) 2.5 l   c) 750 ml   d) 3,000 l

A cuboid has a volume of 240 cm³, is 10 cm long and 6 cm wide. How high is it?

Base area $10 \cdot 6 = 60$ cm², height $240 \div 60 = 4$ cm.

A paddling pool is 2 m long, 1.5 m wide and is filled with water to a height of 30 cm. How many 10-litre buckets is that?

$20 \cdot 15 \cdot 3 = 900$ dm³ = 900 l, so 90 buckets.

If you double all the edges of a cube, how does its volume change? Try it in the widget with 1 → 2 and 3 → 6.

The volume becomes eight times as big: $(2a)^3 = 2 \cdot 2 \cdot 2 \cdot a^3 = 8a^3$. 1 → 8 cubes, 27 → 216 cubes.

How many cm³ are 1 dm³?

UNIT 34 LESSONS

3Surface area and the project “Packaging”

The card for a box is its net. So how much card you need is the area of all six rectangles together, the surface area.

KEY POINT · SURFACE AREA

Each pair of opposite faces is the same size: $a \cdot b$ (top, bottom), $a \cdot c$ (front, back), $b \cdot c$ (left, right). $$O = 2 \cdot a \cdot b + 2 \cdot a \cdot c + 2 \cdot b \cdot c$$

For a cube: $O = 6 \cdot a^2$.

Don’t mix them up: volume in cm³ (cubes), surface area in cm² (squares), edges in cm.

In practice real boxes also need glue flaps, so a little more card.

INTERACTIVE · THE NET AND THE SURFACE AREA
EXAMPLE 5 · WRAPPING PAPER

A present is 30 cm long, 20 cm wide and 10 cm high. What is the least amount of wrapping paper you need?

$O = 2 \cdot 600 + 2 \cdot 300 + 2 \cdot 200 = 2{,}200$ cm² = 22 dm².

at least 2,200 cm²

EXAMPLE 6 · TWO BOXES

Box A measures 16 cm × 2 cm × 2 cm, box B 4 cm × 4 cm × 4 cm. Compare the volume and the amount of card used.

Both have 64 cm³. $O_A = 2 \cdot 32 + 2 \cdot 32 + 2 \cdot 4 = 136$ cm², $O_B = 6 \cdot 16 = 96$ cm².

The cube saves 40 cm² of card.

PROJECT · PACKAGING

Bring in different cuboid-shaped packaging: muesli, juice, tea, toothpaste, shoes.

  1. Measure the edges and calculate the volume and surface area.
  2. Compare with what is really inside. How much air is in the packet?
  3. For each packet, work out how many cm² of card are needed for 100 cm³ of contents. Which is the most economical?
  4. Design a carton for 1 litre of juice that uses as little material as possible, and build a model.
  5. Present your results on a poster. What would you recommend to a manufacturer to cut down packaging waste?

EXERCISES

Calculate the surface area: a) $a = 5$ cm, $b = 4$ cm, $c = 3$ cm   b) cube with $a = 7$ cm   c) $a = 1$ m, $b = 50$ cm, $c = 20$ cm

a) $2 \cdot 20 + 2 \cdot 15 + 2 \cdot 12 = 94$ cm²   b) $6 \cdot 49 = 294$ cm²   c) first in cm: $2 \cdot 5000 + 2 \cdot 2000 + 2 \cdot 1000 = 16{,}000$ cm² = 1.6 m²

A room is 5 m long, 4 m wide and 2.5 m high. The four walls and the ceiling are to be painted. The window and the door together are 6 m². How many m² are painted?

Walls: $2 \cdot 5 \cdot 2.5 + 2 \cdot 4 \cdot 2.5 = 45$ m², ceiling 20 m², without the window and door: $65 - 6 = 59$ m².

Find all the cuboids made of exactly 24 unit cubes (whole-number edges). Which has the smallest surface area?

1×1×24 (98), 1×2×12 (76), 1×3×8 (70), 1×4×6 (68), 2×2×6 (56), 2×3×4 (52). The smallest: $2 \times 3 \times 4$ with 52 cm², the closest to a cube.

TEST YOURSELF!

Surface area of a cuboid with 5 cm, 4 cm, 3 cm?

$2 \cdot (20 + 15 + 12)$

Surface area of a cube with an edge length of 7 cm?

$6 \cdot 49$

REVIEW · DEEPEN · CONNECT

A brick is 24 cm long, 11.5 cm wide and 7.1 cm high. Calculate its volume rounded to whole cm³.

$24 \cdot 11.5 \cdot 7.1 = 1{,}959.6$, so about 1,960 cm³, just under 2 litres.

Connecting with chapter 1.2: Write as a power and calculate: the volume of a cube with a 10 cm edge in cm³, and with a 1 m edge in cm³.

$10^3 = 1{,}000$ cm³ and $100^3 = 10^6 = 1{,}000{,}000$ cm³.

A wooden cube with a 4 cm edge has a small cube with a 1 cm edge cut away at one vertex. How do the volume and surface area change?

Volume: $64 - 1 = 63$ cm³. Surface area: three small squares disappear, but three of the same size are added on the inside: it stays 96 cm².

EXCURSIONTECHNOLOGY

The milk carton: from tetrahedron to cuboid

In the past people bought milk in glass bottles. In Sweden the company Tetra Pak developed a package made of coated card. The first shape was a tetrahedron, a pyramid made of four triangles. In November 1952 a dairy in Lund filled cream into it for the first time, 100 ml per package.

The tetrahedron was easy to fold from a tube of card. But it fits badly into crates and fridges, and a lot of air is left between the packages. That is why the Tetra Brik, a cuboid, came onto the market in 1963. Cuboids can be stacked without gaps, in boxes, on pallets and in lorries. Almost all milk cartons still have this shape today.

Source: Tetra Pak: Heritage / History (tetrapak.com). First machine delivered to the dairy Lundaortens Mejeriförening in September 1952, Tetra Brik introduced in Sweden in 1963.
